blocks.text: The income statement (statement of profit and loss) reports performance **over a period**: what the company earned, what it spent to earn it, and what was left for shareholders. Read it top to bottom as a series of subtotals, each answering a different question.

blocks.text: **Why each subtotal exists.** Gross profit isolates the product economics. EBITDA strips out capital intensity (D&A) and financing (interest), which makes companies with different asset bases and capital structures comparable, and is why EV/EBITDA is the default valuation multiple. EBIT is what the business earns before paying lenders and the government. PAT is what belongs to shareholders and drives EPS and P/E.

items.text: Indian companies present the P&L in the **Schedule III** format of the Companies Act, 2013. It lists expenses by nature (cost of materials consumed, purchases of stock-in-trade, changes in inventories, employee benefits, finance costs, depreciation, other expenses) and **does not show EBITDA or gross profit**. Analysts compute them. Two Indian habits to watch:
**Other income** can be large, especially for cash-rich companies (IT services, FMCG). Keep it out of EBITDA; it is not operating.
**Exceptional items** sit on a separate line before PBT. Read the note: some companies label recurring costs as exceptional to flatter "adjusted" profit.

Below PAT you will also see **other comprehensive income** (actuarial gains, fair value changes on some investments, FX on foreign operations) and **total comprehensive income**. Valuation work almost always uses PAT, not total comprehensive income.

blocks.text: The balance sheet is a **snapshot at a point in time**: what the company owns (assets) and how those assets are financed (liabilities and equity). It always balances because every asset was funded by someone.

items.text: Assets = Liabilities + Shareholders' equity

blocks.text: Group the lines by what they do, not by where they sit:
**Operating assets and liabilities:** PP&E, inventory, receivables, payables, provisions. These generate the business's returns.
**Financing items:** borrowings, lease liabilities, cash, preference capital. These drive net debt and the equity bridge.
**Non-operating assets:** investments, associates, surplus land. These are valued separately.

**Stock versus flow.** The balance sheet shows stocks (balances); the income statement and cash flow statement show flows during the year. Every flow explains a change in a stock. Equity rose from 735 to 900 because PAT of 225 was added and dividends of 60 were paid out.
The cash flow statement explains **why cash changed**. It has three sections:
**Cash from operations (CFO):** cash generated by running the business.
**Cash from investing (CFI):** capex, acquisitions, purchase and sale of investments.
**Cash from financing (CFF):** debt raised or repaid, equity issued, dividends, buybacks, lease principal.
Most companies use the **indirect method**: start from profit, add back non-cash charges, and adjust for working capital movements.

blocks.cap: Figure 4. Profit is an opinion, cash is a fact. The bridge from PAT to the change in cash.

blocks.text: Two derived numbers matter more than any line:
**Free cash flow (FCF)** = CFO − capex = 130. What the business generates after keeping its assets going and growing.
**Cash conversion** = CFO ÷ PAT = 1.24x. Above 1x is normal for a company with meaningful D&A. Persistently below 1x, with rising receivables or inventory, is a red flag.

items.text: Under Ind AS 7, Indian companies usually begin the indirect method from **profit before tax**, add back finance costs and other non-cash items, show **income taxes paid** as a separate operating line, and classify **interest paid under financing**. Lease payments are split: principal in financing, interest per the company's policy. When you compare CFO across companies, check where interest and lease payments sit.

blocks.text: The rules to memorise:
**Net income** is the bottom of the income statement and the top of the cash flow statement.
**Non-cash charges** (D&A, impairment, ESOP cost) reduce net income but are added back in CFO.
**Working capital changes**: an increase in an operating asset uses cash; an increase in an operating liability provides cash.
**Capex** increases PP&E and sits in CFI; **D&A** reduces PP&E.
**Debt issued or repaid** changes borrowings and sits in CFF; **interest** hits the income statement.
**Ending cash** from the cash flow statement is the balance sheet cash.
**Retained earnings** rise by net income and fall by dividends.

blocks.cap: Figure 5. The links that interviewers ask about. Net income starts the cash flow statement; ending cash becomes balance sheet cash; net income less dividends flows into retained earnings.

title.full: WORKED EXAMPLE: DEPRECIATION RISES BY RS. 10

items.text: The single most common accounting question. Assume a 25% tax rate and that the extra depreciation is tax-deductible.
**Income statement:** EBIT falls by 10, so PBT falls by 10. Tax falls by 2.5. **Net income falls by 7.5.**
**Cash flow statement:** net income −7.5, add back depreciation +10. **CFO rises by 2.5.** Nothing else changes, so **cash rises by 2.5**.
**Balance sheet:** assets: PP&E −10, cash +2.5, so total assets −7.5. Equity: retained earnings −7.5. **Both sides fall by 7.5 and it balances.**
The intuition: depreciation is not a cash cost, but it is a tax deduction, so higher depreciation saves tax and *increases* cash.

title.rest: FIVE MORE WALK-THROUGHS TO PRACTISE OUT LOUD
title.full: FIVE MORE WALK-THROUGHS TO PRACTISE OUT LOUD

items.text: Assume 25% tax. Say the answer in the order income statement, cash flow statement, balance sheet.
**Buy inventory of Rs. 100 on credit.** No P&L effect. No cash effect (the working capital increase in inventory is offset by payables). Balance sheet: inventory +100, payables +100.

**Sell that inventory for Rs. 150 cash.** Revenue +150, COGS +100, PBT +50, tax +12.5, NI +37.5. CFO: NI +37.5, inventory decrease +100 → CFO +137.5 (check: the customer paid 150 and tax took 12.5). Balance sheet: cash +137.5, inventory −100; equity +37.5.

**A customer prepays Rs. 120 for a one-year subscription.** At receipt: no revenue; cash +120 (CFO, via increase in deferred revenue); deferred revenue liability +120. As each month passes, revenue of 10 is recognised and the liability falls by 10.

**Raise Rs. 100 of debt at 10% and buy a machine.** Day one: no P&L. CFF +100, CFI −100, cash unchanged. PP&E +100, debt +100. In year one, interest 10 and depreciation (say 10) reduce PBT by 20 and NI by 15.

**Write down goodwill by Rs. 50 (impairment).** PBT −50. Goodwill impairment is usually not tax- deductible, so NI −50 in this case. CFO: add back 50, so no cash effect. Goodwill −50, equity −50. Interviewers often let you assume tax-deductibility for simplicity; state your assumption either way.
**Forgetting tax.** Every income statement change of X changes net income by X × (1 − tax rate).
**Wrong sign on working capital.** Receivables up means customers have not paid you yet: that uses cash.
**Putting interest in the wrong place.** Interest expense is an income statement item; debt principal repayment is not.
**Saying "EBITDA is cash flow".** It ignores working capital, capex, interest and tax. A fast-growing distributor can have strong EBITDA and negative operating cash flow.

blocks.text: **Accrual accounting** records revenue when it is earned and expenses when they are incurred, not when cash moves. That timing gap is what working capital measures.

blocks.text: **Ind AS 115: revenue from contracts with customers** uses a five-step model:
Identify the **contract** with the customer.
Identify the **performance obligations** (distinct promises: a phone and a two-year service plan are two).
Determine the **transaction price**, including variable consideration such as discounts, rebates and penalties.
**Allocate** the price to each obligation using standalone selling prices.
Recognise revenue **when (or as) each obligation is satisfied**: at a point in time (control transfers, as for a product sale) or over time (as for construction, SaaS or long-term services).

Why interviewers care: revenue recognition is where earnings are most often managed. Principal-versus-agent judgements (does an e-commerce platform book gross merchandise value or only its commission?), bill-and-hold arrangements, and aggressive percentage-of-completion estimates can all inflate reported revenue.

title.rest: WHY A GROWING COMPANY CAN RUN OUT OF CASH
title.full: WHY A GROWING COMPANY CAN RUN OUT OF CASH

items.text: A distributor grows sales 40% a year. It must pay suppliers in 30 days but gives dealers 90 days' credit, and it holds 60 days of stock. Every extra Rs. 100 of annual sales ties up roughly Rs. 100 × (60 + 90 − 30) ÷ 365 = **Rs. 33 of working capital**. Profitable growth can therefore consume more cash than the profit it produces, and the company must borrow. This is the answer to "can a profitable company go bankrupt?": yes, if it runs out of cash.

title: Working capital and the cash conversion cycle

blocks.text: **Net working capital (NWC)** = operating current assets − operating current liabilities. Exclude cash and debt; they are financing items. For Kaveri: receivables 160 + inventory 220 − payables 200 − other current liabilities 80 = **Rs. 100 crore**.
The **cash conversion cycle (CCC)** measures how many days cash is tied up between paying suppliers and collecting from customers.

items.text:
DSO = Receivables ÷ Revenue × 365 = 29.2 days
DIO = Inventory ÷ COGS × 365 = 73.0 days
DPO = Payables ÷ COGS × 365 = 66.4 days
CCC = DSO + DIO − DPO = 35.8 days

blocks.cap: Figure 6. Kaveri's cycle: 102 days to turn raw material into cash, 66 of them financed by suppliers.

blocks.text: **Levers and their cash value.** Cutting inventory by 10 days releases COGS ÷ 365 × 10 = **Rs. 30 crore** of cash, permanently. That is why working capital programmes appear in every PE 100-day plan and every CFO's agenda.

items.text: **"Operating cycle versus cash conversion cycle: what is the difference?"** The operating cycle is DIO + DSO: days from buying inventory to collecting cash. The cash conversion cycle subtracts DPO, the part the suppliers finance. A strong answer adds that negative CCC is a source of funding for growth, and a sudden rise in DSO is often the first sign of channel stuffing or customer stress.

title: D&A, impairment, goodwill, intangibles, leases and share-based pay

blocks.text: These items share two features: they involve **management judgement**, and they are mostly **non-cash** in the year they are recorded. Both make them favourite interview material and favourite places to hide problems.

**Depreciation and amortisation.** Capex is spread over an asset's useful life: straight-line (equal each year) or written-down value (a fixed percentage of the declining balance). The Companies Act (Schedule II) gives indicative useful lives. Tax depreciation under the Income-tax Act uses its own block-wise WDV rates, which creates **deferred tax**.

**Impairment (Ind AS 36).** If an asset's carrying amount exceeds its **recoverable amount** (the higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use), it is written down. Goodwill and indefinite-life intangibles are tested **every year**. Impairments are non-cash but signal that a past acquisition or investment destroyed value.

**Goodwill (Ind AS 103).** Purchase price − fair value of identifiable net assets acquired. Under Ind AS it is **not amortised**, only tested for impairment. A large goodwill balance tells you the company has grown by acquisition.

Intangibles (Ind AS 38). Customer lists and technology bought in an acquisition are recognised and amortised; acquired brands with an indefinite life are not amortised but tested for impairment every year. Internally generated brands are not recognised. Research is expensed; development is capitalised only when strict criteria are met, which is why software and pharma companies' capitalisation policies deserve scrutiny.

**Leases (Ind AS 116).** Lessees recognise a **right-of-use asset** and a **lease liability** for almost all leases. Rent disappears from operating expenses and is replaced by depreciation and interest.

title.rest: A RS. 30 CRORE ANNUAL LEASE UNDER IND AS 116
title.full: WORKED EXAMPLE: A RS. 30 CRORE ANNUAL LEASE UNDER IND AS 116

items.text: A retailer signs a 10-year store lease at Rs. 30 crore a year; the incremental borrowing rate is 9%.
Lease liability and ROU asset at start = 30 × annuity factor (9%, 10 years) = **Rs. 192.5 crore**.
Year 1 depreciation = 192.5 ÷ 10 = 19.3; interest = 192.5 × 9% = 17.3. Total charge **36.6** versus rent of 30: front-loaded.
**EBITDA rises by 30** because rent is no longer an operating expense. Net debt rises by 193 if you include lease liabilities.

Implications: compare airlines, retailers and hospitals on **EBITDAR** or on consistent pre- or post-Ind AS 116 EBITDA, and keep the EV bridge consistent. If EBITDA excludes rent, EV must include lease liabilities. An interviewer asked a candidate exactly this: "How would you adjust the balance sheets of an airline that leases aircraft versus one that owns them?"

blocks.text: **Share-based payments (Ind AS 102).** ESOPs are expensed at grant-date fair value over the vesting period. The cost is non-cash but real: it transfers value from existing shareholders. Be sceptical of "adjusted EBITDA excluding ESOP cost", common among Indian new-age companies, and always use **diluted** shares in valuation.

items.text: Treating all non-cash charges as irrelevant. ESOP cost is a real cost; impairment is evidence of past overpayment.
Forgetting that capitalising a cost raises EBITDA today and depreciation later. Rising capitalised development costs with flat revenue is a warning sign.
Mixing pre- and post-Ind AS 116 numbers when comparing multiples across years or peers.

Kaveri consolidates 100% of the subsidiary's revenue, EBITDA and PAT, then deducts **Rs. 10 crore attributable to non-controlling interests** to arrive at profit attributable to Kaveri's shareholders. EPS and P/E use the attributable figure; EV/EBITDA uses consolidated EBITDA with NCI added to EV.

blocks.text: **Deferred tax (Ind AS 12)** arises from temporary differences between book and tax values. The classic case: tax depreciation faster than book depreciation creates a **deferred tax liability** (tax deferred to later years). Carry-forward losses and provisions not yet deductible create **deferred tax assets**, which are recognised only if future taxable profit is probable. Ind AS uses the balance sheet approach: compare carrying amounts with tax bases.

**One-offs and normalisation.** Restructuring costs, asset sale gains, litigation settlements, inventory write-downs and FX gains distort a single year. For valuation, build a **normalised** or "run-rate" profit, but be consistent: if you strip out one-off costs, strip out one-off gains too, and ask whether "one-off" items recur every year.

title: Reading an Indian annual report: Ind AS, audit opinion, notes and segments

blocks.text: **Ind AS versus IFRS.** Indian Accounting Standards are converged with IFRS, with a small number of **carve-****outs**. You do not need every carve-out; know that they exist and the common ones:
Presentation follows **Schedule III** of the Companies Act rather than a free-form IFRS layout.
**Business combinations under common control** (group restructurings) use pooling of interests (Ind AS 103, Appendix C).
A **bargain purchase gain** goes to capital reserve rather than profit.

**Applicability**: listed companies and unlisted companies above net worth thresholds use Ind AS. **Banks** still report under Indian GAAP and RBI norms, and insurers follow IRDAI formats, so their statements look different.{{verify}}

**The audit report.** Read it first. An **unmodified** opinion is the norm. A **qualified** opinion, an **adverse** opinion or a **disclaimer** is serious. Also read **Key Audit Matters** (areas of highest judgement), any **Emphasis of Matter** (for example, going concern), and the **CARO 2020** annexure (fixed assets, inventory verification, loans to related parties, defaults). An **auditor resignation** mid-term is a major red flag; SEBI's LODR regulations require the reasons to be disclosed.
**The notes that matter most in an interview or diligence:**
Significant accounting policies (revenue, capitalisation, useful lives).
**Segment information (Ind AS 108)**: revenue, profit and capital employed by business or geography, as management sees them.
Borrowings: maturities, rates, security, covenants.
**Related party transactions (Ind AS 24)**: loans, royalties, purchases with promoter entities. Material related party transactions need shareholder approval under LODR Regulation 23.{{verify}}
**Contingent liabilities and commitments**: tax disputes are common in India and can be large.
Leases, employee benefits (gratuity), ESOPs, and subsequent events.

**"Walk me through the three financial statements."** A strong 60-second answer: "The income statement shows revenue, expenses and profit over a period, ending with net income. The balance sheet shows assets, liabilities and equity at a point in time, and must balance. The cash flow statement starts with net income, adjusts for non-cash items and working capital to get cash from operations, then adds investing and financing flows to explain the change in cash. They link through net income, which flows into the cash flow statement and retained earnings, and through ending cash, which becomes balance sheet cash."

**Follow-up to expect:** "If you could look at only one statement to judge a company, which?" A defensible answer is the cash flow statement, because it is hardest to manipulate and shows whether profits convert to cash; mention that you would still want the balance sheet to check leverage and liquidity.

items.text:
ROE  = PAT ÷ shareholders' equity = 225 ÷ 900 = 25.0%
ROCE = EBIT ÷ (equity + debt) = 320 ÷ 1,300 = 24.6%
ROIC = EBIT × (1 − tax) ÷ (equity + debt − cash) = 320 × 0.75 ÷ 1,150 = 20.9%

blocks.text: Use **average** capital (opening plus closing, divided by two) when the balance sheet moves a lot during the year. On average equity, Kaveri's ROE is 27.5%. Indian investors quote **ROCE** heavily; global investors and consultants prefer **ROIC** because it is after tax and excludes idle cash.
**DuPont analysis** splits ROE into three levers so you can see whether returns come from margins, efficiency or borrowing:

blocks.cap: Figure 7. DuPont decomposition of Kaveri's ROE. The same 25% ROE could come from a thin-margin, fast-turning retailer or a high- margin, asset-heavy manufacturer.

items.text: **Value is created only when return on capital exceeds the cost of capital.** Growth multiplies whatever spread you have: growth at ROIC above WACC creates value; growth at ROIC below WACC destroys it faster. This one sentence answers a surprising number of interview questions.

title.full: WORKED EXAMPLE: GROWTH THAT DESTROYS VALUE

items.text: Two companies each have Rs. 1,000 crore of capital and a 12% cost of capital.
**Company A** earns 20% ROIC. Economic profit = (20% − 12%) × 1,000 = **+Rs. 80 crore** a year. Investing another Rs. 100 crore at 20% adds Rs. 8 crore a year of economic profit.

**Company B** earns 9% ROIC. Economic profit = (9% − 12%) × 1,000 = **−Rs. 30 crore** a year. If B grows capital 20% a year at the same ROIC, its reported profit rises but its economic loss grows too.

An interviewer who asks "high sales growth but low ROCE, or slow growth but high ROCE?" is testing exactly this. The strong answer: prefer the high-ROCE business unless you can show the low-ROCE company is in a temporary investment phase (new plants not yet at capacity) and its incremental returns are rising.
Questions from recent Indian campus interviews, with the logic interviewers wanted:

**"Two companies: one has higher gross margin, the other higher EBITDA margin. Which do you invest in? You may ask one more question."** Gross margin shows product and pricing power; EBITDA margin shows the cost structure after overheads and marketing. A high-gross, low-EBITDA company may be investing in brand-building (future operating leverage) or may be bloated. Ask for **return on capital employed** or **cash conversion**, because margins without capital intensity do not tell you about value.

**"If ROE is lower than ROCE, would you as an equity investor welcome new debt?"** Compare like with like (post-tax). ROE = ROIC + (ROIC − post-tax cost of debt) × D/E. If ROE is below ROIC, the business is earning less than its debt costs, so more debt lowers equity returns further. Welcome debt only if it funds projects with returns above the cost of debt and risk stays manageable.

**"How does an expansion affect ROCE?"** In the short run it falls: capital rises immediately (capital work-in-progress, new plant) while earnings arrive only as utilisation ramps up. Judge expansions on incremental ROCE at maturity.

**"If you could look at only three ratios, which?"** A good set: ROCE or ROIC (quality), revenue or EPS growth (trajectory), and cash conversion (honesty of earnings). Add net debt/EBITDA if the business is leveraged.

items.text: A startup sells software to small clinics at Rs. 5,000 a month with an 80% gross margin. It spends Rs. 90,000 to acquire each customer. Monthly churn is 2%.
Monthly gross profit per customer = 5,000 × 80% = Rs. 4,000.
Simple CAC payback = 90,000 ÷ 4,000 = **22.5 months**. With churn, it takes longer (see chart).
LTV = 4,000 ÷ 2% = **Rs. 2,00,000**; LTV/CAC = **2.2x**. Workable, but below the 3x comfort level: the company should cut churn or CAC before scaling spend.

**Cement:** realisation per tonne, cost per tonne (raw material, power and fuel, freight), EBITDA per tonne, capex per tonne of capacity. A strong answer compares a company's EBITDA per tonne with peers and explains the gap (limestone proximity, fuel mix, logistics).
**Quick-service restaurants and retail:** revenue per store, same-store sales growth, store-level EBITDA margin, payback on a new store's capex.
**Hospitals:** average revenue per occupied bed (ARPOB), occupancy, EBITDA per bed, capex per bed.
**Lending:** net interest margin, credit cost, operating cost to assets, return on assets per loan product.

title.rest: HOW TO PROJECT REVENUE IN AN INTERVIEW OR PITCH
title.full: HOW TO PROJECT REVENUE IN AN INTERVIEW OR PITCH

items.text: Start from how the company reports (investor presentation segments).
Pick the two or three drivers that explain most of the history (for example volume growth and realisation).
Tie each driver to an external anchor: industry volume growth, capacity additions, price trends, GDP or consumption data.
Triangulate bottom-up (drivers) with top-down (market size × share) and with consensus estimates.
Sanity-check against the company's own 3 to 5 year history. If you forecast faster growth than it has ever achieved, say why.

blocks.text: Two companies with the same reported profit can deserve very different valuations. **Quality of earnings** asks how much of reported profit is recurring, cash-backed and fairly measured.

**Signs of high quality:** recurring revenue from many customers, CFO consistently close to or above PAT, stable accounting policies, conservative capitalisation, a normal tax rate, clean audit reports.
**Red flags to scan for in every annual report:**
Receivables or inventory growing much faster than revenue.
CFO persistently below PAT; profits never turn into cash.
Rising capitalised costs (development, interest) with flat revenue.
Frequent "exceptional" or "one-off" charges that recur.
Large or growing related party transactions.

items.text: **Rs. 1 lakh at 12% for 10 years** grows to about Rs. 3,10,585: roughly 3.1x. Rule of 72: money doubles in about 72 ÷ 12 = 6 years.
**A perpetuity of Rs. 100 a year at 10%** is worth Rs. 1,000. If the payment grows at 4%, it is worth 104 ÷ (10% − 4%) ≈ Rs. 1,733.
**A home loan of Rs. 50 lakh at 9% for 20 years** has an EMI of about Rs. 44,986 a month (monthly rate 0.75%, 240 payments).
**Revenue grew from 500 to 800 in 4 years**: CAGR = 1.6^(0.25) − 1 ≈ 12.5%.
**Nominal return 12%, inflation 5%**: real return ≈ 1.12 ÷ 1.05 − 1 ≈ 6.7%. Always discount nominal cash flows at nominal rates and real at real.

blocks.text: **Compounding frequency.** Monthly compounding at 12% a year is an effective annual rate of 1.01^12 − 1 = 12.68%. Indian fixed deposits quote quarterly compounding; bonds usually semi-annual. Convert before comparing.

**Net present value** is the sum of all cash flows discounted at the cost of capital. Positive NPV means the project earns more than investors require. **Internal rate of return** is the discount rate at which NPV equals zero.

title: Cost of capital: CAPM, beta and WACC

blocks.text: The **discount rate must match the cash flow**: free cash flow to the firm (available to debt and equity holders) is discounted at the **weighted average cost of capital**; free cash flow to equity is discounted at the **cost of equity**. The rate must also match the currency (rupee cash flows, rupee rates) and the inflation basis (nominal with nominal).

Pre-tax cost of debt  Kd = yield on new debt

blocks.text: **Each input, and where to get it in India:**

**Risk-free rate (Rf).** The 10-year Government of India bond yield, about **7.1 to 7.2%** in late September 2026 (it touched a two-year high near 7.18%).{{verify}} Match the maturity to the cash flows.

**Equity risk premium (ERP).** Aswath Damodaran's January 2026 estimate for India is a total ERP of **7.08%**: a mature-market premium of 4.23% plus a country risk premium of 2.85% (India rated Baa3 by Moody's). Indian practitioners commonly use 6 to 8%. Be consistent: if your rupee risk-free rate already includes India's default spread, adding a full country premium partly double counts.

**Beta.** Regress stock returns on the Nifty (2 to 5 years of weekly or monthly data), or better, take peers' betas, **unlever** them, take the median, and **relever** at your company's target debt-to-equity. Bloomberg's adjusted beta = 0.67 × raw + 0.33 × 1 pulls estimates towards 1.

**Cost of debt.** Yield to maturity on the company's listed bonds, or the government bond yield plus a spread for its credit rating, or current bank borrowing rates. Use the marginal rate on new debt, not the historical average coupon.
**Weights.** Use **target** market-value weights, not book values.

Pre-tax cost of debt 8.5%; after 25% tax = **6.38%**.

blocks.text: **Capital structure theory in one paragraph.** Modigliani and Miller showed that in a world without taxes or distress costs, financing mix does not change firm value: cheaper debt is exactly offset by riskier (costlier) equity. With taxes, debt adds value through the **interest tax shield** (present value ≈ tax rate × debt for permanent debt). Beyond some point, expected **costs of financial distress** outweigh the shield, which gives an optimal range, not a point. The **pecking order** view adds that managers prefer internal cash, then debt, then equity, because issuing equity signals that shares may be overvalued. **Adjusted present value (APV)** values the business unlevered and adds the tax shield separately; it is useful when leverage changes over time, as in LBOs.

Adding a country risk premium on top of a rupee risk-free rate without thinking.
Forgetting that more debt raises the cost of equity, so WACC does not keep falling as debt rises.
Saying "beta can never be negative". It can (gold miners, some hedges), but it is rare for operating companies.

blocks.text: Every valuation or investment case rests on a handful of uncertain assumptions. Good analysts show **how much the answer moves** when those assumptions move, and **which ones matter most**.
**Sensitivity analysis** flexes one or two inputs at a time. Excel's Data Table builds two-way grids (WACC against terminal growth, entry against exit multiple).

**Scenario analysis** changes several related assumptions together into internally consistent stories: base, upside, downside (for example, a demand slowdown lowers volume, price and margin together).
**Tornado charts** rank inputs by their impact on the answer, so discussion focuses on what matters.
**Break-even analysis** finds the volume or revenue at which profit is zero.

blocks.text: **Operating and financial leverage.** The **degree of operating leverage** (DOL) = % change in EBIT ÷ % change in sales = contribution ÷ EBIT. The **degree of financial leverage** (DFL) = % change in EPS ÷ % change in EBIT = EBIT ÷ (EBIT − interest). Their product, the combined leverage, tells you how much EPS swings for a 1% move in sales. At revenue of Rs. 1,000 crore in the break-even example, contribution is 400 and EBIT is 100, so DOL = 4: a 10% fall in revenue cuts EBIT by 40%.

There are three families of valuation. **Intrinsic** (DCF): value is the present value of future cash flows. **Relative** (trading comparables and precedent transactions): value is what the market pays for similar assets. **Contingent claim** (option pricing): value of assets whose payoff depends on an uncertain event, such as an undeveloped oil field or a patent. Bankers show all the relevant ones side by side in a **football field**.

blocks.text: **Equity value** (market capitalisation for a listed company) is the value of the shareholders' claim. **Enterprise value** is the value of the operating business to all capital providers: shareholders, lenders and other claimants. The bridge between them is the most tested valuation concept.

items.text:
Enterprise value = Equity value (diluted) + Debt + Lease liabilities + Preference capital + Non-
controlling interest − Cash and liquid investments − Associates and JVs − Other non-operating
assets

blocks.cap: Figure 13. The bridge in numbers for an illustrative listed company.

blocks.text: **The logic of each item.** Add every claim on the operating business that is not common equity (debt, leases, preference shares). Add **NCI** because consolidated EBITDA includes 100% of subsidiaries you only partly own. Subtract **cash** because a buyer effectively gets it back. Subtract **associates and JVs** because their earnings are not in EBITDA. Consider adding **debt-like items**: unfunded gratuity or pension deficits, large provisions, deferred acquisition payments, and for Indian companies, significant contingent liabilities you judge likely to crystallise.

**The rule of consistency.** EV multiples use metrics available to all capital providers (revenue, EBITDA, EBIT, FCFF). Equity multiples use metrics after interest (PAT, EPS, book value, FCFE). Never divide EV by net income or market cap by EBITDA.

**Diluted shares.** Use the **treasury stock method** for in-the-money options and warrants: assume they are exercised and the company uses the cash to buy back shares at the current price. Example: 10 crore basic shares, price Rs. 100, 1 crore options with strike Rs. 60. Exercise raises Rs. 60 crore, which buys back 0.6 crore shares, so diluted shares = 10 + 1 − 0.6 = **10.4 crore**. Convertible bonds use the **if-converted method** when the conversion price is below the share price.

items.text: **"A company raises Rs. 100 crore of debt and holds the cash. What happens to EV and equity value?"** Nothing to either at the moment of the raise: debt rises by 100 and cash rises by 100, so net debt is unchanged. Equity value may change later if the market thinks the debt will be used well or badly.
**"It then uses the cash to buy back shares."** Equity value falls by 100 (fewer shares at the same price, ignoring signalling); net debt rises by 100; EV is unchanged.
**"Can equity value exceed enterprise value?"** Yes, when cash and non-operating assets exceed debt, for example a cash-rich IT services company.
**"Why add minority interest?"** Because EBITDA consolidates 100% of the subsidiary; to compare like with like, EV must include the value of the part you do not own.

**"Company A buys Company B. What are the combined EV and equity value?"** It depends on the funding. With cash: combined equity value ≈ A's equity value (cash left, B's equity was bought); combined EV ≈ EV(A) + EV(B) + any premium paid. With stock: combined equity ≈ equity(A) + purchase price paid in new shares. Walk through each claim; the interviewer wants the method, not a formula.

blocks.text: **Trading comparables** value a company by the multiples at which similar listed companies trade. The four decisions that make or break a comps analysis:

**Peers.** Same business model, end market, growth and margin profile, size and geography. Start from the company's own filings (who it names as competitors), analyst reports, and the DRHPs of recently listed peers.
**Multiple.** Pick the one that reflects how the sector is valued and what drives value.
**Period.** Last twelve months (LTM) or forward (FY27E, FY28E). Use the same period for all peers. Forward multiples dominate in India for growing companies.
**Statistic.** Median and interquartile range, not the mean (outliers distort it).

title.full: WORKED EXAMPLE: VALUING KAVERI ON COMPARABLES

items.text: Kaveri's FY27E EBITDA is Rs. 467 crore (14% growth, 20.5% margin). At the median 21.0x, EV = Rs. 467 × 21.0 ≈ Rs. 9,815 crore. Less net debt of Rs. 250 crore gives equity of about Rs. 9,565 crore, or **Rs. 191 per share**. Using the interquartile range (19.5x to 24.0x) gives **Rs. 177 to 219**.

Kaveri actually trades at Rs. 165: 18.2x FY27E EBITDA (21.2x LTM) and 36.7x LTM earnings. That is about 13% below the peer median on the same forward basis, although its growth (14%) is the joint highest in the set and its margin is above the median. A strong answer would explain the discount (smaller scale? lower liquidity? governance?) before calling it undervalued.

blocks.text: What drives a multiple. Multiples are compressed DCFs. For a stable company, forward P/E = payout ratio ÷ (cost of equity − growth), and EV/EBITDA rises with growth and return on capital and falls with risk. So when a peer trades at a premium, the explanation must be higher growth, higher returns, lower risk, or mispricing. Say which.

items.text: Mixing LTM and forward multiples, or calendar and fiscal years (Indian companies report April to March).
Using P/E to compare companies with very different leverage.
Including a peer at 80x because it is "the market leader" and letting the mean do the work.
Forgetting that a company with large cash looks expensive on P/E and cheap on EV/EBITDA, or the reverse with heavy debt.

blocks.cap: Figure 14. The seven steps of a DCF.

blocks.text: **Step 1: forecast.** Build revenue from drivers, then margins, capex, depreciation and working capital. Five to ten years, long enough for the company to reach a steady state. Kaveri uses seven years, with growth fading from 14% to 8% and EBITDA margin expanding from 20.5% to 23% on scale.
**Step 2: free cash flow to the firm.**

items.text: FCFF = EBIT × (1 − tax) + D&A − Capex − Increase in NWC

blocks.text: **Step 3: discount at WACC** of 12.1% (chapter A3). Kaveri uses the **mid-year convention** (cash arrives through the year, so year one is discounted by half a year).
**Step 4: terminal value.** Two methods, which you should use to cross-check each other:
**Perpetuity growth (Gordon):** TV = FCFF₍n+1₎ ÷ (WACC − g). Long-term growth must not exceed long-run nominal GDP growth; for India, 5 to 7% nominal is a common range.
**Exit multiple:** TV = final-year EBITDA × an exit EV/EBITDA multiple. Simple but imports today's market mood into the far future.

The subtle point that separates strong candidates: growth needs reinvestment. In steady state, reinvestment rate = g ÷ return on new capital. Kaveri assumes 6% growth and a 30% return on new capital, so it must reinvest 20% of NOPAT: FCFF₍n+1₎ = NOPAT 626 × (1 − 20%) = 501. Terminal value = 501 ÷ (12.07% − 6.0%) = Rs. 8,260 crore. If you naively grow the last explicit FCFF, you implicitly assume a 60% return on new capital and overstate value by about 9% (Rs. 117 versus Rs. 107 per share).
**Step 5 to 7: enterprise value to price.**

Figure 16. Value per share across WACC and terminal growth.

blocks.text: **Sanity checks before you trust any DCF:**

Terminal value share of 60 to 80% is common for a 5 to 10 year forecast. Treat more than about 80% as a warning (the campus rule of thumb for a 5-year forecast): most of the value then sits beyond the years you actually modelled.
**Implied exit multiple** should be plausible for a mature version of the company.
**Terminal ROIC and reinvestment** must be consistent with growth.
**Asset turnover** should not rise implausibly as you grow.

**Reverse DCF:** what does the market price imply? Kaveri trades at Rs. 165; even at a WACC of 11.1% and 7% terminal growth our DCF gives about Rs. 149. The market is pricing faster or longer growth, or a lower discount rate, than our base case. That tension is the heart of a good stock pitch.

items.text: **"Walk me through a DCF."** "I project the company's free cash flow to the firm for five to ten years: EBIT after tax, plus D&A, less capex and working capital investment. I discount those at the WACC, estimate a terminal value with either a perpetuity growth rate or an exit multiple, discount that back, and add them to get enterprise value. Then I subtract net debt and other claims to get equity value and divide by diluted shares for a value per share, which I compare to the market price with sensitivities on the key assumptions."

**Follow-ups that come up in Indian interviews:** "What terminal growth did you use and why? Nominal or real?" (nominal, to match nominal cash flows and WACC). "Why is there a gap between your perpetuity and exit multiple terminal values?" (the exit multiple embeds market growth and return expectations; reconcile them). "When would you not use a DCF?" (banks and insurers, where debt is raw material, so use FCFE, DDM or P/B-ROE; early startups with no visibility; distressed companies; highly cyclical firms without normalisation).

title: Precedent transactions, control premium, synergies and cycles

blocks.text: **Precedent transactions** value a company using multiples paid in past acquisitions of similar businesses. They usually exceed trading multiples because they include a **control premium**: the buyer gets to set strategy, capture synergies and control cash flows. Premiums over the undisturbed share price are often in the 20 to 40% range globally, and vary widely with competition and market conditions.

**Revenue synergies** (cross-selling, pricing, distribution) are uncertain and slow; **cost synergies** (procurement, overlapping overheads, plants) are more reliable. Buyers who pay away all expected synergies in the premium transfer the value to the seller's shareholders.
**Precedents age.** A deal done at the top of a cycle or in a zero-rate world may not be a fair guide today.
**Deal context matters.** Distressed sales, minority stakes, strategic versus financial buyers and stock versus cash consideration all change the multiple.

items.text: In India, acquiring 25% or more of a listed company (or control) triggers a **mandatory open offer** for at least another 26% under SEBI's Takeover Regulations (SAST, 2011). The offer price must be at least the highest of several benchmarks, including the negotiated price and recent volume-weighted market prices. This rule shapes Indian deal structures (share purchase plus open offer, as in UltraTech's acquisition of India Cements in 2024 and Torrent Pharma's of JB Chemicals in 2025) and puts a floor under the price minority shareholders receive.

blocks.text: **Cyclicals.** For cement, steel, chemicals and commodities, using peak or trough earnings misleads. Use **normalised** mid-cycle margins, EV/capacity (EV per tonne), or replacement cost, and check where you are in the capacity cycle.

title: Valuation ranges, the football field and common pitfalls

blocks.cap: Figure 17. Kaveri football field. Market multiples justify today's price; a disciplined DCF does not. The recommendation must explain that gap.

blocks.text: A **football field** puts every method's range on one chart against the current or offer price. Present a range, then a view: "We think fair value is Rs. X to Y; the market price implies Z; the key swing factor is..."
**The pitfalls interviewers probe:**
**Double counting.** Adding cash to a DCF that already earns interest income in EBIT; including leases in EV but using pre-Ind AS 116 EBITDA.
**Dilution ignored.** Using basic shares when ESOPs and convertibles are material.
**Inconsistent periods and currencies.** FY versus CY; rupee cash flows with a dollar WACC.
**Equity value from EV multiples of a loss-maker.** Negative EBITDA makes the multiple meaningless; use revenue or a DCF.

**Holding companies.** Indian conglomerates often trade at a **holding company discount** to the sum of their listed parts. A sum-of-the-parts (SOTP) valuation should apply one, and explain it (cash leakage, capital allocation risk, tax on distributions).

title.rest: WHY BANKS TRADE ON PRICE TO BOOK
title.full: WHY BANKS TRADE ON PRICE TO BOOK

items.text: For a bank in steady state, a justified price-to-book multiple is:
P/B = (ROE − g) ÷ (Ke − g)

A bank with ROE 16%, growth 10% and cost of equity 13% deserves P/B = 6 ÷ 3 = **2.0x**. The same bank at ROE 12% deserves only 0.67x. That is why Indian private banks with high, stable ROEs trade at multiples of book while weaker banks trade below book. A DCF on FCFF does not work for banks because deposits and borrowings are their raw material, not financing.

blocks.text: **Special situations.**
**Startups and loss-makers:** value a future steady state (revenue × steady-state margin × multiple, discounted back at a venture-style rate), or use comparable funding rounds; see Part E.
**Distressed companies:** liquidation value, recovery analysis by creditor class, or a DCF on a restructured balance sheet.
**Digital platforms:** value per user or per transaction, with cohort-based lifetime value.
**Real options:** mines, pharma pipelines and licences can be valued as options; mention this only if the interviewer goes there.

blocks.text: **Primary versus secondary.** A **primary** issue creates new shares and the money goes to the company (fresh issue, QIP, rights, preferential allotment). A **secondary** sale transfers existing shares and the money goes to the selling shareholders (offer for sale in an IPO, OFS on the exchange, block deals). Interviewers ask "who gets the money?" constantly.

**Dilution.** Issuing new shares reduces existing holders' percentage ownership. Whether it reduces **value** per share depends on price and use of proceeds: raising equity at a fair price to fund projects that earn more than the cost of capital is value-accretive even though ownership falls.

items.text: A stock trades at Rs. 100. The company announces a **1-for-4 rights issue at Rs. 80**.
**Theoretical ex-rights price (TERP)** = (4 × 100 + 1 × 80) ÷ 5 = **Rs. 96**.
Value of each right = TERP − subscription price = 96 − 80 = **Rs. 16**.

A shareholder with 4 shares either subscribes (pays 80, ends with 5 shares worth 480 = 400 + 80) or sells the entitlement for about 16. Either way, **no value is lost** if the market prices correctly. The discount is not a gift; it is a transfer that shareholders capture by subscribing or selling their rights.

**Anchor book in IPOs:** from 30 November 2025, 40% of the anchor portion is reserved for domestic institutions (33% for mutual funds and 7% for insurers and pension funds), up from one-third earlier, and larger issues may have more anchor investors (Part B).

**Large-issuer rules:** minimum public offer and minimum public shareholding norms were eased for very large issuers in March 2026, allowing smaller initial floats with longer timelines to reach 25% public shareholding. This is why mega-IPOs such as NSE's in September 2026 can list with a small float.
Rights issues became much faster from April 2025, and are now a serious alternative to QIPs; rights issue fund-raising rose sharply in 2025 as QIPs slowed.

**Buybacks** changed twice: open-market buybacks were stopped in April 2025 and reintroduced from August 2026, and **Budget 2026** moved buyback taxation back to capital gains for shareholders (from April 2026), with an extra tax on promoters.

**"Why would a company choose a QIP over a rights issue?"** Speed and certainty: a QIP can close in days with a few large institutions, while a rights issue needs all shareholders' participation and promoters' support. The rights issue avoids diluting existing shareholders who subscribe and can be priced at a deeper discount. Promoters who want to maintain their stake prefer rights; companies wanting new institutional shareholders prefer QIPs.

**"Fresh issue or OFS: which is better for the company?"** Only the fresh issue brings money into the company. A large OFS component tells investors that existing holders (often PE funds or promoters) want to sell, which is fine for a mature business but raises questions if the company needs growth capital.

**"Why do buybacks increase EPS?"** They reduce shares outstanding; if the lost interest income on cash (after tax) is smaller than the earnings attributable to the retired shares, EPS rises. Whether value rises depends on buying below intrinsic value.

title: Bonds, yields, duration, spreads and covenants

blocks.text: A bond's price is the present value of its coupons and principal at the market yield. **Price and yield move in opposite directions.** Yield to maturity is the single discount rate that equates price with those cash flows.

items.text: At a market yield of 7.2%, price = **98.61** per 100 of face value (below par because the coupon is below the yield).
**Macaulay duration** (weighted average time to cash flows) = 7.50 years; **modified duration** = 6.99. A 0.5% rise in yield should cut the price by about 6.99 × 0.5% ≈ 3.5%.
Actual price at 7.7% = 95.24; at 6.7% = 102.14. The price rises more when yields fall than it drops when yields rise: that asymmetry is **convexity**, which bondholders like.

blocks.cap: Figure 19. Price against yield: the duration line is a tangent; the true curve bends above it.

blocks.text: **Credit spread** is the extra yield over a government bond of the same maturity, compensating for default risk and illiquidity. It depends on the **credit rating** (AAA, AA, A, BBB are investment grade; BB and below are high yield) and on market conditions. India's main rating agencies are CRISIL, ICRA, CARE Ratings and India Ratings.

**Covenants** protect lenders: **maintenance** covenants (net debt/EBITDA below 3x, interest cover above 3x, tested quarterly) and **incurrence** covenants (limits on new debt, dividends, asset sales). Breaching one gives lenders the right to accelerate repayment, which is why treasurers track covenant headroom (Part C).

title: Dividends, buybacks, leverage, refinancing and liquidity

blocks.text: **Payout policy** answers what to do with cash the business cannot reinvest at returns above its cost of capital. The options:
**Dividends** are sticky: companies are reluctant to cut them, so a dividend increase signals confidence. In India they are taxed in shareholders' hands at slab rates.

**Buybacks** are flexible and can signal that management thinks the shares are undervalued. After Budget 2026, shareholders are again taxed on buyback proceeds as capital gains, while promoters face an additional levy, which narrows the tax arbitrage promoters used to enjoy.
**Debt paydown** reduces risk and interest cost; right when leverage is above target or rates are high.
**Holding cash** preserves optionality but drags on ROE and ROCE; shareholders dislike idle cash without a plan.

**Refinancing risk** is the risk that maturing debt cannot be rolled over on acceptable terms. A company with most of its debt maturing in one year is fragile even if its leverage looks moderate. **Liquidity** is the ability to meet obligations as they fall due: cash, undrawn committed facilities and predictable operating cash flow.

**Model conventions every reviewer expects:**
**Structure:** cover and contents, an assumptions sheet, the three statements, supporting schedules (revenue build, capex and depreciation, working capital, debt), valuation, and a checks sheet.
**Colour code:** blue font for hard-coded inputs, black for formulas, green for links to other sheets. Never hard-code a number inside a formula.
**One row, one formula:** the same formula across a row so it can be audited.
**Timeline** across columns, clearly labelled historical (A) and forecast (E), in Indian fiscal years (April to March).
**Checks:** balance sheet balances every year; cash flow ending cash equals balance sheet cash; debt never negative. A model that does not balance fails the test regardless of anything else.
**Circularity:** interest on average debt creates a circular reference with cash. Use a circuit-breaker switch or interest on opening balances.
**Avoid** OFFSET , INDIRECT and merged cells in shared models; they break easily and are hard to audit.

items.text: In India, **merchant bankers** registered with SEBI manage public issues (the "book running lead managers" or BRLMs on an IPO). blocks.text: **Teaser versus CIM.** The teaser is short and anonymous: business description, key financials, investment highlights; its job is to get NDAs signed. The CIM is detailed and confidential: history, products, customers, operations, management, historical and projected financials; its job is to support a non-binding offer.

**Signing versus closing.** Signing is when the definitive agreement is executed; closing is when ownership and money actually change hands, after conditions precedent are met. In India the gap can be months if CCI or RBI approval or an NCLT scheme is required.

On the buy side the bank helps a client **screen** targets, value them, structure and finance the deal, run diligence and negotiate. A typical buy-side sequence: strategic rationale → target screening → approach (often through the target's promoter or bankers) → indicative offer → diligence → financing commitments → binding offer and SPA → approvals → closing → integration. Your value as the buy-side adviser is discipline: an independent valuation, a clear walk-away price, and early identification of deal-breakers.

title.full: INDIA LENS: HOW INDIAN DEALS ARE STRUCTURED

items.text: **Share purchase** of an unlisted company: SPA plus SHA; stamp duty on share transfer.

**Acquisition of a listed company:** acquiring 25% or more of voting rights, or control, triggers a **mandatory open offer** for at least 26% more under SEBI's Takeover Regulations (SAST 2011). Creeping acquisitions of up to 5% a year are allowed between 25% and the maximum non-public holding. Deals are often a **share purchase plus open offer**, sometimes followed by a merger or delisting.

**Mergers and demergers** through a **scheme of arrangement** under sections 230 to 232 of the Companies Act, approved by shareholders, creditors, stock exchanges (for listed companies) and the **NCLT**; can take 6 to 12 months.
**Business transfer / slump sale:** a business undertaking sold for a lump sum; different tax treatment.

**Merger control:** CCI approval is needed above asset or turnover thresholds and, since September 2024, for deals with a **transaction value above Rs. 2,000 crore** where the target has substantial business operations in India.{{verify}}
**Cross-border:** FEMA pricing guidelines, sectoral FDI caps and Press Note 3 (government approval for investors from countries sharing a land border with India).

**Acquisition finance:** RBI's 2026 directions allow banks, from 1 April 2026, to finance acquisitions of control by Indian companies (up to 75% of deal value, acquirer net worth of at least Rs. 500 crore, post-deal consolidated debt-to-equity no more than 3:1), a big change from the earlier restriction.

title: Accretion and dilution, purchase price allocation and synergies

blocks.text: **Accretion/dilution analysis** asks: after the deal, is the acquirer's EPS higher or lower than it would have been alone? Boards care because markets watch EPS, though EPS accretion is not the same as value creation.

items.text:
Pro forma EPS = (Acquirer NI + Target NI − after-tax interest on new debt − lost interest on cash
used − after-tax amortisation of new intangibles + after-tax synergies) ÷ (Acquirer shares + new
shares issued)

title.full: WORKED EXAMPLE: KAVERI BUYS A SNACKS COMPANY

items.text: Kaveri (net income Rs. 225 crore, 50 crore shares, EPS Rs. 4.50; for this exercise assume it trades at 20x P/E, so Rs. 90 a share) buys a target earning Rs. 30 crore for Rs. 450 crore (15x earnings), paying half in stock and half with new debt at 9%.
New shares = 225 ÷ 90 = **2.5 crore**.
After-tax interest on Rs. 225 crore of debt = 225 × 9% × 0.75 = **Rs. 15.2 crore**.
**Accretive by 1.5%.**

**The shortcut:** compare the target's **earnings yield** at the purchase price (30 ÷ 450 = 6.7%) with the acquirer's **weighted cost of acquisition currency**: 50% × Kaveri's earnings yield (1 ÷ 20 = 5.0%) + 50% × after-tax cost of debt (6.75%) = 5.88%. The target yields more than the currency costs, so the deal is accretive.

**Now pay 25x, all in stock:** price Rs. 750 crore needs 8.33 crore new shares; EPS falls to Rs. 4.37, a change of **-2.9%** (dilutive). The board would need about **Rs. 10 crore of pre-tax synergies** a year to break even.

blocks.cap: Figure 24. Accretion or dilution across price and funding mix. Paying more and using more stock pushes the deal into dilution.

blocks.text: **Rules of thumb interviewers expect:**
In an **all-stock** deal, the deal is accretive if the acquirer's P/E is **higher** than the P/E paid for the target. A low-P/E company buying a high-P/E company with stock is dilutive.
In an **all-cash** (or debt) deal, compare the target's earnings yield with the after-tax cost of debt or the forgone interest on cash.
Accretion is not value creation: a deal can be accretive and still destroy value if the price exceeds what the target is worth to the buyer.
**Purchase price allocation (Ind AS 103).** At closing, the buyer records the target's identifiable assets and liabilities at fair value; the excess of price over that is goodwill.

items.text: Price Rs. 450 crore. Target book net assets Rs. 150 crore. Fair value step-ups: customer relationships and brand Rs. 120 crore, PP&E Rs. 30 crore. Deferred tax liability on the step-ups = 150 × 25% = 37.5.
Fair value of net assets = 150 + 150 − 37.5 = **Rs. 262.5 crore**.
**Goodwill = 450 − 262.5 = Rs. 187.5 crore**, tested annually for impairment.
The finite-life intangibles are amortised, which reduces future EPS: include that amortisation in accretion/dilution analysis.

blocks.text: **The cast.** The **issuer** and its board; **book running lead managers** (the banks); legal counsel for the issuer, the banks and any selling shareholders; statutory auditors; the **registrar**; the stock exchanges; **SEBI**; a **monitoring agency** (a credit rating agency) to track the use of fresh-issue proceeds; and investors.

**The documents.** The **DRHP** (draft red herring prospectus) is filed with SEBI and the exchanges and made public for comments; it contains the business description, industry report, risk factors, objects of the issue, restated financials, capital structure, legal proceedings and management discussion. SEBI issues **observations**, which the issuer addresses. The **RHP** (red herring prospectus) is filed with the Registrar of Companies before marketing and has everything except the final price. The **prospectus** is filed after pricing. Since 2022, companies may also use a **confidential pre-filing** route, keeping the draft private until closer to launch.

**Eligibility.** Under Regulation 6(1) of the ICDR Regulations, an issuer must meet track-record tests (net tangible assets, average operating profit of at least Rs. 15 crore over the preceding three years, net worth). Companies that do not, typically loss-making new-age companies, list under **Regulation 6(2)** with at least 75% of the issue allocated to QIBs.
**Allocation (Regulation 6(1) issuers).**

blocks.text: **Anchors.** Anchor investors are allotted at a fixed price one day before the issue opens, which signals quality to the rest of the book. Their shares are locked in: 50% for 30 days and 50% for 90 days. From 30 November 2025, 40% of the anchor portion is reserved for domestic mutual funds (33%) and insurers and pension funds (7%).

**Price band and bidding.** The price band is announced at least two working days before opening; the cap can be at most 120% of the floor. Bidding runs for at least three working days through **ASBA** (application supported by blocked amount) and UPI. After the issue closes (T), allotment is finalised on T+1, shares are credited and refunds processed on T+2, and trading starts on **T+3**.

**Lock-ins after listing.** Promoters must hold at least 20% of post-issue capital as the **minimum promoter contribution**, locked in for 18 months (three years if proceeds fund capex); promoter holding above that, and pre-IPO shareholders' holdings, are locked for six months.

**Use of proceeds.** General corporate purposes are capped at 25% of the fresh issue (35% combined with unidentified acquisitions). For Regulation 6(2) issuers, large existing shareholders face limits on how much they can sell in the OFS.

In a book-built issue, investors bid a quantity at prices within the band. The lead managers build the **demand curve** and, with the issuer, set the final price, usually at the top of the band when demand is strong.

blocks.text: **What bankers look at beyond the headline subscription:** the quality and price sensitivity of QIB demand (long-only funds versus hedge funds), how much demand is at the cut-off price, anchor book composition, grey market chatter (unofficial and unreliable), and whether the pricing leaves something on the table for a healthy listing. A deal priced so aggressively that it falls on listing damages the bank's and the issuer's reputation.

title: Fresh issue, offer for sale and dilution

blocks.text: A **fresh issue** creates new shares; money goes to the company; all existing shareholders are diluted.
An **offer for sale (OFS)** sells existing shares; money goes to the selling shareholders; no new shares are created and total share count is unchanged.

Most Indian IPOs combine both. Large recent IPOs were often entirely OFS: Hyundai Motor India (October 2024, about Rs. 27,870 crore, India's largest IPO), LG Electronics India (October 2025, about Rs. 11,600 crore) and the National Stock Exchange (September 2026, about Rs. 22,560 crore). Tata Capital (October 2025, about Rs. 15,500 crore) combined a large fresh issue with an OFS.

title.rest: WHO OWNS WHAT AFTER THE IPO
title.full: WORKED EXAMPLE: WHO OWNS WHAT AFTER THE IPO

items.text: Before the IPO, a company has 10 crore shares: the promoter owns 7.5 crore (75%) and a PE fund 2.5 crore (25%). It IPOs at Rs. 500 with a **fresh issue of Rs. 1,000 crore** (2 crore new shares) and an **OFS of 1.5 crore shares by the PE fund** (Rs. 750 crore, which goes to the fund).
Post-issue shares = 10 + 2 = **12 crore**; market cap at issue = **Rs. 6,000 crore**.
The company receives Rs. 1,000 crore; its post-money net cash rises by that amount (less issue expenses). The promoter's stake is diluted by the fresh issue only.

blocks.text: Once listed, companies raise money through **QIPs** (fast, institutions only), **rights issues** (existing holders, now completed in about 23 working days), **preferential allotments** (named investors, shareholder approval, pricing floor), and **FPOs** (full public offering). Shareholders sell through **OFS on the exchange** and **block deals**. Chapter A5 compares them in detail.
Two cases worth knowing:
**Vodafone Idea's FPO** (April 2024, Rs. 18,000 crore) is India's largest follow-on public offer, used to fund network investment for a heavily indebted telecom company.

**Adani Enterprises' FPO** (early 2023, Rs. 20,000 crore) was fully subscribed and then withdrawn after a short-seller report hit the share price, a lesson in market risk between pricing and allotment.

**Buybacks and open offers** are the other side of ECM: bankers (where appointed) manage **tender offer** buybacks, the reintroduced open-market buybacks, and **open offers** triggered under the Takeover Regulations. The key questions are purpose (return surplus cash, signal value, consolidate control), price relative to market, acceptance ratios, and tax, which changed with Budget 2026.

**"Who gets the money in an OFS?"** The selling shareholders. The company gets nothing, but bears part of the process cost only if agreed.

**"Why do promoters of profitable companies do IPOs that are mostly OFS?"** Liquidity and exit for early investors, price discovery for future fund-raising, brand and governance benefits, and meeting minimum public shareholding norms.

blocks.text: **A typical rated NCD issue:** mandate → credit rating process (management meetings with the rating agency, rating rationale published) → term sheet (size, tenor, coupon, security, covenants, call/put options) → investor sounding → pricing through the stock exchange **electronic book provider (EBP)** platform for private placements → allotment and listing → ongoing servicing. The DCM banker's craft is reading investor appetite: the right tenor and structure can save many basis points.

Acquisition finance funds a purchase with debt serviced by the combined business. Lenders look at **leverage** (debt/EBITDA), **interest cover**, **free cash flow to service debt**, **security** (share pledge, assets), and **sponsor or acquirer equity** at risk.

Structures in India have historically relied on NBFCs, offshore lenders and holding company NCDs, because Indian banks could not generally finance the purchase of shares. RBI's 2026 directions opened bank acquisition finance for control transactions by eligible Indian companies, with limits on the bank-funded share of the deal and on post-deal leverage. Expect interviewers at banks with lending arms to ask how this changes deal activity and competition with private credit funds.

items.text: **"What would you look at to decide whether a company can issue a five-year bond?"** Business stability, EBITDA and cash flow coverage of interest and principal, leverage against peers and rating thresholds, existing maturities, security, covenants, and the rating outcome that the market will price.

**"Should a company fund an acquisition with debt or equity?"** Debt if cash flows are stable, leverage stays within target, and the acquirer's shares are undervalued; equity if the target is risky, leverage is already high, or the acquirer's shares are richly valued (currency is expensive to them, cheap to the seller).

blocks.text: **Driver-based planning** builds the plan from operating drivers rather than last year plus a percentage: outlets × throughput × price for revenue; headcount × cost per head for staff costs; utilisation for capacity. It makes forecasts explainable and scenarios quick.

blocks.cap: Figure 30. A KPI tree links EBITDA to drivers that individual managers own.

blocks.text: Variance analysis explains the gap between plan and actual in terms of drivers. For revenue, the standard split is **volume, mix and price**:

items.text:
Volume variance = (Actual total units − Budget total units) × Budget average price
Mix variance    = Σ (Actual units of product − Actual total units × Budget mix %) × Budget price
Price variance  = Σ (Actual price − Budget price) × Actual units
Budget revenue = **Rs. 84.0 crore**; actual = **Rs. 83.9 crore**. Revenue looks flat, but the drivers tell a different story:
**Volume +4.2:** we sold 105 lakh units against 100, valued at the budget average price of Rs. 84.
**Mix -5.2:** the mix shifted from premium A (budget 60%) to value B (actual 52% B), which cost more than the extra volume added.
**Price +0.9:** A's price rose Rs. 4 (+2.0 crore), B's fell Rs. 2 (−1.1 crore).

**The commentary a CFO wants:** "Revenue was flat against budget because a shift towards the value pack offset 5% higher volumes. The premium pack lost 10 lakh units after a competitor's launch in the south; we are testing a promotional response and will update the full-year forecast by Rs. 3 to 4 crore lower unless share recovers by November." That sentence names the driver, the cause, the consequence and the action.

blocks.cap: Figure 31. The same variance as a bridge.

blocks.text: **Cost variances** follow the same logic: headcount variance (number of people) versus rate variance (cost per head); for materials, usage variance versus price variance. Always separate **timing** (a cost that slipped a month) from **permanent** variances, and **one-offs** from run-rate changes.
**Scenarios** combine consistent assumptions: a monsoon failure lowers rural volumes, raises input costs and delays price increases together.
**Sensitivities** show the impact of one driver: a 1% rupee depreciation, a 5% rise in crude, a 10-day increase in receivable days.

**Forecast accuracy** is tracked by the error between forecast and actual (mean absolute percentage error) and **bias** (always too high or too low). A team that always forecasts high is telling you something about incentives.

blocks.text: **Contribution margin** (price minus variable cost) is the unit of analysis. Fixed costs do not change with a pricing decision in the short run, so compare options on contribution.

title.rest: HOW MUCH VOLUME CAN WE LOSE AFTER A PRICE INCREASE?
title.full: HOW MUCH VOLUME CAN WE LOSE AFTER A PRICE INCREASE?

items.text: A product has a 40% contribution margin. If we raise price by 5%, the volume we can lose before total contribution falls is:
Break-even volume loss = price increase ÷ (contribution margin + price increase) = 5% ÷ 45% = 11.1%

If market research suggests volume falls by only 4 to 6%, the increase adds contribution. The same formula in reverse tells you how much extra volume a price cut must generate: a 5% cut needs 5% ÷ (40% − 5%) = 14.3% more volume just to stand still.

blocks.text: **Customer and channel profitability** allocate cost-to-serve (discounts, trade spend, logistics, credit days, returns) to each customer or channel. In Indian consumer businesses, **general trade** (kirana stores via distributors), **modern trade** (supermarkets), **e-commerce** and **quick commerce** have very different margins, credit terms and trade spend. A channel that looks large and fast-growing can be unprofitable after cost-to-serve.

**The capex approval process:** business case (strategic rationale, demand, capacity) → financial evaluation (NPV, IRR, payback, sensitivities) → risks and alternatives → approval at the right level (plant, CFO, board depending on size) → execution → **post-investment review** comparing actuals with the approved case.

title.full: WORKED EXAMPLE: A NEW PRODUCTION LINE

items.text: A Rs. 120 crore line is expected to generate cash flows of 25, 32, 38 and then 40 a year for years 4 to 7. At a 12% hurdle rate:
**NPV = Rs. 41.4 crore**; **IRR = 21.4%**; payback ≈ **3.6 years**.
If volumes are 20% lower than planned, NPV falls to **Rs. 9.1 crore**: still positive, but thin.
The tornado chart in chapter A3 shows volume is the assumption to diligence; the recommendation should include a volume trigger for a phased build.

blocks.text: **Make-or-buy** compares the incremental cost of making (materials, labour, variable overheads, incremental fixed costs, capital) with buying (supplier price, logistics, quality and supply risk). Strategic factors often decide: control of quality or intellectual property, supplier concentration, and flexibility.

title: Sales, supply chain and plant finance

blocks.text: **Standard costing:** each product has a standard cost (materials, labour, overheads at standard rates and quantities). Variances (price, usage, efficiency, volume) show where the plant is gaining or losing money.

**Absorption versus marginal costing:** absorption costing loads fixed overheads into inventory, so producing more than you sell can raise reported profit in the short term. Marginal costing avoids this, and is better for decisions.
**Inventory valuation** (weighted average or FIFO under Ind AS 2; LIFO is not permitted) affects margins when input prices move.
**Sales finance:** trade spend effectiveness, schemes and discounts, distributor margins and credit, sales force productivity.

items.text: **"Sales grew 12% but EBITDA fell. What happened, and what would you do?"** Structure the answer: (1) confirm facts: one-offs, accounting changes, acquisitions; (2) revenue quality: price versus volume versus mix; discount and trade spend growth; channel mix; (3) gross margin: input costs, product mix, pricing lag; (4) operating costs: marketing, people, freight, new capacity costs; (5) conclude with the two or three drivers that explain most of the gap and a recommended action for each. Finance interviewers reward the structure and a quantified conclusion more than any single right answer.

blocks.text: The **13-week cash flow forecast** is treasury's core tool: a week-by-week view of receipts (customer collections by due date) and payments (suppliers, salaries, taxes, interest, capex), rolled forward every week. It shows the timing of cash gaps and gives time to act.

blocks.cap: Figure 32. A 13-week forecast. The balance breaches the Rs. 60 crore buffer in weeks 6 and 7 and again from week 10, when a tax payment and a capex milestone coincide with slower collections.

blocks.text: What treasury does with that chart: draw on a committed revolving credit facility for weeks 6 to 13, issue short-term commercial paper, accelerate collections (early-payment discounts, factoring through TReDS platforms for MSME receivables), negotiate supplier timing, or defer a discretionary payment. The lowest point is **Rs. 27 crore in week 11**.

**Working capital levers:** tighter credit terms and collections discipline (receivables), better demand planning and SKU rationalisation (inventory), and supplier terms and supply chain finance (payables).

items.text: **Paying small suppliers late now costs tax.** Section 43B(h) of the Income-tax Act disallows a deduction for amounts owed to micro and small enterprises until paid, if payment exceeds the MSMED Act limit (45 days with an agreement). This changed payables management across Indian companies from FY24.{{verify}}
**TReDS** platforms let MSME suppliers discount invoices on large buyers, a common supply chain finance tool.

Surplus cash is typically invested in bank deposits, liquid and overnight mutual funds, commercial paper and treasury bills under a board-approved investment policy (safety, then liquidity, then yield).

blocks.text: **Debt maturity profile.** Spread maturities so no single year carries a refinancing wall; match debt tenor to asset life; keep committed undrawn facilities as a liquidity buffer.

items.text: A company's loan requires net debt/EBITDA of at most 3.0x. Net debt is Rs. 600 crore and EBITDA is Rs. 250 crore, so leverage is 2.4x. EBITDA can fall to 600 ÷ 3.0 = Rs. 200 crore, a **20% decline**, before the covenant is breached. Treasury reports this headroom monthly and runs it through downside scenarios; if a breach looks likely, it negotiates a waiver or amendment early rather than late.

blocks.text: **FX risk.** Three types: **transaction** (a dollar payable or receivable), **translation** (consolidating foreign subsidiaries), **economic** (competitiveness when the rupee moves). Hedging tools: forwards, options, and natural hedges (matching dollar costs with dollar revenues).

items.text: An Indian importer owes US$10 million in three months. Spot is Rs. 96.00 per dollar; three-month rupee and dollar interest rates are 6.5% and 4.5%. The forward rate is about **Rs. 96.47**. Buying dollars forward locks the rupee cost at about Rs. 96.5 crore, whatever happens to the rupee. The forward premium reflects the interest rate differential; it is not a forecast. An option costs a premium upfront but keeps the upside if the rupee strengthens.

blocks.text: **Interest rate risk:** floating-rate borrowers are exposed to rate rises; fixed-rate borrowers to rate falls (opportunity cost). Interest rate swaps convert one into the other. Treasury's rate view matters: in September 2026 Indian 10-year yields had risen to about 7.2% with the repo rate at 5.25%.

blocks.text: **Internal financial controls.** The Companies Act requires boards to report on internal financial controls, and auditors of most companies to opine on them. Controls cover authorisation (who can approve what), segregation of duties, reconciliations, system access and review. When controls fail, you get errors, fraud and restatements; interviewers like asking how you would detect a problem, such as "revenue booked but not delivered" (reconcile invoices with dispatch records and customer confirmations; check credit notes after period end).

**Quarterly and annual reporting for listed companies.** Under SEBI's LODR Regulations, quarterly results are due within 45 days of quarter end (60 days for the fourth quarter and annual audited results), approved by the audit committee and board, with a limited review or audit by the statutory auditor.

blocks.text: **What the grid teaches:**
**Entry price is the biggest lever you control.** Buying at 9x instead of 10x lifts IRR by about 5 points in this example.
**Never underwrite multiple expansion.** Build the base case at an exit multiple equal to or below entry.
**Leverage amplifies both ways.** More debt raises IRR if the business performs and destroys equity if it does not.
**Time kills IRR.** The same MOIC over a longer hold means a lower IRR, which is why funds sell good businesses.

items.text: The interviewer gives: EBITDA, entry multiple, leverage, growth, sometimes margins and capex. Work it like this:
**Entry:** EV = EBITDA × multiple; equity = EV + fees − debt.
**EBITDA at exit:** grow at the given rate (10% for 5 years ≈ ×1.6; 15% ≈ ×2.0).
**Cash generated:** yearly FCF ≈ net income + D&A − capex − ΔNWC, where net income = (EBITDA − D&A − interest) × (1 − tax). Sum it over the hold and subtract it from the entry debt.
**Exit equity:** exit EBITDA × exit multiple − remaining debt.
**Returns:** MOIC = exit equity ÷ entry equity; convert to IRR with rules of thumb: **2x in 3 years ≈ 26%**, **2x in 5 years ≈ 15%**, **2.5x in 5 years ≈ 20%**, **3x in 5 years ≈ 25%**.

**"What makes a good LBO candidate?"** Stable, predictable cash flows; low capex needs; strong market position and pricing power; room to improve operations; a clear exit route; assets or cash flows that lenders will lend against; a reasonable price.

**"Why might a hospital be a poor LBO candidate while a software company can be a good one?"** A question from a recent interview. A new hospital needs heavy capex and years to ramp up occupancy, so cash flow cannot service debt early. A mature, recurring-revenue software business with high margins and low capex generates steady cash to repay debt (though mature hospital chains with stable occupancy do attract buyouts).

**"How does leverage increase returns, and what are the risks?"** The sponsor puts in less equity for the same asset, and cash flow repays debt, so equity captures all the upside. Risks: covenant breaches, refinancing, and wiping out equity in a downturn.

title: Growth equity: ownership, preferences and exit waterfalls

blocks.text: Most Indian PE deals are **minority growth investments**: the fund buys 10 to 40% alongside the promoter, often with a mix of **primary** capital (to fund growth) and **secondary** purchases (from earlier investors).
**Ownership math:** post-money = pre-money + new money; investor stake = new money ÷ post-money. A Rs. 300 crore primary investment at a Rs. 1,200 crore pre-money valuation buys 300 ÷ 1,500 = 20%.

**Instruments:** compulsorily convertible preference shares (CCPS) are standard: they convert into equity (often at a ratio that adjusts to performance targets) and carry a **liquidation preference** that pays the investor back first in a sale.
**Returns come from growth, not leverage:** earnings growth and exit multiple drive the outcome; there is little or no debt paydown.
**Protections:** board seat, affirmative votes on budgets, acquisitions and new issues; anti-dilution; tag-along and drag-along; exit rights through an IPO within a set period.

items.text: A **Rs. 1,000 crore** fund wants to return **3x gross, Rs. 3,000 crore**. Suppose it owns on average **10%** of its companies at exit (after dilution from later rounds).

blocks.cap: Figure 47. TAM, SAM and SOM for a clinic software startup.

items.text: A startup sells practice-management software to clinics.
TAM: about 2.5 lakh clinics × Rs. 60,000 a year (Rs. 5,000 a month) = Rs. 1,500 crore.
SAM: 40% are digitised enough and located in cities the company can serve = Rs. 600 crore.
SOM: winning 5% of SAM in five years = Rs. 30 crore of revenue.

Now the venture question: at a 10x revenue multiple, Rs. 30 crore of revenue is worth Rs. 300 crore, far below the Rs. 10,000 crore outcome a Rs. 1,000 crore fund needs. Unless the company can expand (payments, lending to clinics, pharmacy, insurance, other countries), this is a good business but not a venture-scale one. That is the reasoning interviewers want to hear.

blocks.text: **Top-down check:** start from a published market size, apply the relevant share and penetration. If bottom-up and top-down differ by 5x, find out why.
**Founder-market fit:** why these founders for this problem: domain experience, unique insight, access to customers, technical depth.
**Execution evidence:** speed of shipping, hiring quality, ability to sell, how they handled setbacks. Reference calls with former colleagues and customers.
**Product insight:** what they know that others do not; the "earned secret".
**Defensibility over time:** network effects, proprietary data, switching costs, brand, scale economics, regulation. Early on, speed is the only moat; ask what moat the company will have at scale.
**Competition:** incumbents, other startups, global players entering India. "We have no competition" is a red flag.

Signs of **product-market fit**: retention curves that **flatten** rather than decay to zero; organic and word-of-mouth growth; customers who complain when the product breaks; rising usage per user; improving unit economics as the company scales; newer cohorts that retain better than older ones.

blocks.text: **Growth quality:** is growth bought (discounts, paid marketing) or earned (referrals, organic)? Is it concentrated in a few customers or cities? Does it survive when discounts are removed?

items.text: **Seed.** Founders hold 1 crore shares.
