The investor gets 20%, the pool 10%, and founders **70%**: the pool comes entirely out of the founders' share. Price per share ≈ Rs. 17.5.

**Series A.** A lead invests **Rs. 20 crore at Rs. 80 crore pre-money** (20% for Series A) and again asks for the pool to be topped up to 10% **post-money**, in the pre-money. After the round: founders **54.4%**, seed **15.6%**, pool **10.0%**, Series A **20%**.

Because the pool top-up comes out of the pre-money, the **effective pre-money** for existing shareholders is only about **Rs. 77.8 crore**, not Rs. 80 crore. Founders negotiating a round should compare offers on effective pre-money, not headline pre-money.

title: Liquidation preference, anti-dilution and control rights

blocks.text: **Liquidation preference** decides who gets paid first in a sale. A **1x non-participating** preference gives the investor the greater of its money back or its share of proceeds as if converted. A **participating** preference gives both: money back first, then its share of what remains.

blocks.cap: Figure 50. Series A (Rs. 20 crore for 20%) payout at different exit values.

blocks.text: At a **Rs. 50 crore** exit: non-participating Series A takes Rs. 20 crore (its preference beats 20% × 50 = 10); participating takes 20 + 20% × 30 = Rs. 26 crore. Founders and others share the rest.
Above a **Rs. 100 crore** exit, non-participating Series A converts, because 20% of the exit exceeds Rs. 20 crore.
The preference matters most in **modest exits**, which are the most common kind.
**Anti-dilution** protects investors if a later round is priced lower (a down round):
**Full ratchet:** the old investor's conversion price drops to the new price. Harsh on founders.

**Broad-based weighted average (standard):** new conversion price = old price × (A + B) ÷ (A + C), where A = shares outstanding before the round, B = shares the new money would buy at the old price, C = shares actually issued. With 10 lakh shares outstanding, a Rs. 1 crore round at Rs. 50 instead of the old Rs. 100: B = 1 lakh, C = 2 lakh, new price = 100 × 11 ÷ 12 = **Rs. 91.7**, not Rs. 50.

**Other terms:** pro rata rights (right to invest in future rounds to maintain ownership), board seats and observer rights, information rights, protective provisions (investor consent for new share issues, sale of the company, changes to rights), right of first refusal and co-sale, drag-along and tag-along, founder vesting (commonly four years with a one-year cliff), ESOP pool size, and exclusivity (no-shop) during diligence.

After investing, the VC joins the board or observes, helps with hiring, customers and the next round, and reviews milestones. The **follow-on decision** is where fund returns are made: double down (use reserves to keep ownership) when the company is breaking out and the new price still leaves room for a large multiple; hold when progress is ambiguous; stop when the thesis is broken. Exits come through **strategic sales**, **secondary sales** to later investors, **IPOs** (increasingly common in India) and, for most startups, shutdowns. Fund performance is attributed company by company: which decisions (initial pick, ownership, follow-on) drove returns.

items.text: **"A startup raises Rs. 50 crore at a Rs. 200 crore pre-money. What does the investor own?"** 50 ÷ 250 = 20%.

**"Why do VCs ask for an option pool in the pre-money?"** It shifts the dilution from the new investor to existing holders and lowers the effective pre-money. Founders can negotiate the pool's size to a hiring plan.
**"Which matters more, valuation or terms?"** In most outcomes, terms: a higher valuation with a participating 2x preference can leave founders worse off than a lower valuation with clean terms.

blocks.text: A case interview is a structured conversation about a business problem. The skills: clarify the objective, build a **MECE** (mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive) structure, prioritise, do quick maths, and synthesise a recommendation.
**Frameworks worth knowing (use them as prompts, not scripts):**
**Profitability:** profit = revenue (price × volume, by segment) − costs (fixed, variable). Where did the change happen, why, what to do.
**Market entry:** market attractiveness (size, growth, profitability, competition), our ability to win (capabilities, economics), mode of entry (build, buy, partner), risks.
**M&A / PE diligence:** market, target's position, financials and quality of earnings, synergies or value creation, price and returns, risks and deal-breakers.

items.text: **Prompt:** "A PE fund is considering buying a chain of 120 diagnostic labs in western India for Rs. 1,800 crore. Should it?"
**Market:** diagnostics demand growth (ageing, chronic disease, insurance penetration), share of organised players, competitive intensity from national chains and online aggregators.

blocks.text: Project finance funds a single asset (a road, power plant, renewable park, airport) through a **special purpose vehicle** whose debt is repaid only from the project's cash flows, with limited or no recourse to sponsors. Risks are allocated by contract: construction risk to the EPC contractor, operating risk to the O&M operator, demand or price risk to the offtaker through a long-term PPA or concession.

items.text: A solar project generates cash available for debt service of **Rs. 120 crore a year**. Lenders require a minimum DSCR of **1.3x** and offer a 12-year loan at 9%.
Maximum annual debt service = 120 ÷ 1.3 = **Rs. 92.3 crore**.
Maximum debt = 92.3 × annuity factor (9%, 12 years) = 92.3 × 7.16 ≈ **Rs. 661 crore**.
If the project costs Rs. 900 crore, sponsors must provide about Rs. 239 crore of equity (about 27%).
